sections.name: Section A — Multiple Choice
sections.instructions: Choose ONE correct answer. Each question is worth 2 points.

questions.question: Which symbol starts a comment in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses # to start a single-line comment.

questions.question: What does df.head() show?
questions.explanation: df.head() returns the first 5 rows by default.

questions.question: What does df.shape return?
questions.explanation: df.shape returns a (rows, columns) tuple.

questions.question: Which library is used to work with data tables in Python?
questions.explanation: pandas is the data-table library; numpy is for arrays.

questions.question: What does np.mean([2, 4, 6]) return?
Which function reads a CSV file in pandas?
questions.explanation: pd.read_csv() is the standard CSV reader.

questions.question: When you use sklearn's built-in datasets (like load_iris), which is true?
options: You need to upload a file
questions.explanation: sklearn's built-in datasets ship with the library.

questions.question: Why do we split data into train and test?
options: To check the model honestly on data it has never seen
questions.explanation: The test set is the honest exam — data the model never saw during training.

questions.question: In train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25), what is the train size?
questions.explanation: test_size=0.25 means 25% test, so 75% train.

questions.question: What does random_state=42 do?
options: Makes the split the SAME every time you run the code
Sets accuracy to a fixed value
questions.explanation: random_state fixes the random seed for reproducibility.

questions.question: If you test a model on the SAME data it was trained on, what happens?
options: The score will be too LOW
The score will be too HIGH (the model already saw the answers)
The score will be exactly right
The model will not train at all
questions.explanation: Testing on training data is cheating — the model has seen the answers, so the score is overoptimistic. This is the core reason we hold out a test set.

questions.question: Which model does NOT need feature scaling?
questions.explanation: Tree-based models split on thresholds, so the scale of features does not matter.

questions.question: Why does a Decision Tree NOT need scaling?
options: Trees only use Yes/No questions — the scale does not matter
questions.explanation: Tree splits like x > 5 work the same way at any scale.

questions.question: Linear Regression predicts:
questions.explanation: Linear Regression is for predicting continuous numbers.

questions.question: Logistic Regression predicts:
questions.explanation: Despite the name, Logistic Regression is for classification.

questions.question: A Decision Tree makes predictions by:
options: Asking a series of Yes/No questions
questions.explanation: A tree walks down a chain of yes/no questions to reach a leaf.

questions.question: Random Forest is:
questions.explanation: A 'forest' = many trees combined by voting/averaging.

questions.question: A Decision Tree picks the BEST split by choosing the question that:
options: Uses the column with the highest average
Makes the two groups the CLEANEST (lowest Gini)
Splits the data exactly in half
Uses the median of the column
questions.explanation: The tree tries every possible split and picks the one with the lowest Gini (cleanest groups).

questions.question: Why is Random Forest more stable than a single Decision Tree?
options: Forests do not need training data
Many trees vote and cancel out each other's mistakes
questions.explanation: Bagging: errors of individual trees average out when many trees vote.

questions.question: MAE stands for:
questions.explanation: MAE = Mean Absolute Error.

questions.question: Lower MAE means:
questions.explanation: Lower error = better predictions.

questions.question: If MAE = 5 and RMSE = 15 for the same model, what does this tell you?
options: Most mistakes are small, but at least one is HUGE
questions.explanation: A large gap RMSE >> MAE means uneven errors — one or more big mistakes are pulling RMSE up.

questions.question: R² = 0 means:
options: The model is no better than just guessing the average
questions.explanation: R² = 0 means your model performs the same as the lazy 'always-the-average' model.

questions.question: Accuracy is:
questions.explanation: Accuracy = correct / total.

questions.question: When does accuracy LIE?
options: When the data is IMBALANCED (one class is rare)
When the model is too small
questions.explanation: On imbalanced data, a model that always predicts the majority class looks great by accuracy but is useless.

questions.question: Precision answers:
options: How many real YES cases did we catch?
When the model says YES, how often is it right?
questions.explanation: Precision = TP / (TP + FP).

questions.question: Recall answers:
options: When the model says YES, how often is it right?
Of all real YES cases, how many did we catch?
questions.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN).

questions.question: For cancer detection, which metric matters MOST?
questions.explanation: Missing a real cancer case (false negative) is the most costly mistake — so we maximise recall.

questions.question: F1 score is high only when:
options: BOTH precision AND recall are high
Either precision OR recall is high
questions.explanation: F1 is the harmonic mean — it pulls down to the smaller of precision and recall.

questions.question:
Look at this confusion matrix (row = real, col = predicted; class 1 = PASS):
[[40, 10],
 [ 5, 45]]
What is the accuracy?
questions.explanation: Correct = 40 + 45 = 85. Total = 100. Accuracy = 0.85.

sections.name: Section B — Fill in the Blanks
sections.instructions: Write your answer in the box. One word or a short phrase is enough.

questions.question: The function in sklearn that splits the data into train and test parts is called:
questions.explanation: from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

questions.question: In model.fit(X, y), the variable X is the [BLANK 1] and y is the [BLANK 2].
questions.explanation: X = features/clues, y = target/label.

questions.question:
Complete the import line:
from [BLANK 1] import [BLANK 2]
(to bring LogisticRegression from sklearn)
questions.explanation: from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

questions.question: A model that does NOT learn anything and always predicts the same value (like always 'not spam') is called the ___ model. (Starts with L or B.)
questions.explanation: We call it the lazy / baseline / dummy model — the floor that real models must beat.

questions.question: If 95 emails are normal and only 5 are spam, the data is ___ (one word).
questions.explanation: Imbalanced data — one class is much rarer than the other.

questions.question: Fill in the missing word: 'RMSE is similar to MAE, but it ___ big mistakes (counts them extra).'
questions.explanation: RMSE punishes/penalizes big mistakes because of the squaring step.

questions.question:
Look at this confusion matrix (row 0 = really NO, row 1 = really YES):
[[40, 10],
 [ 5, 45]]
[BLANK 1] = number of false alarms (FP)
[BLANK 2] = number of missed cases (FN)
questions.explanation: FP = top-right = 10. FN = bottom-left = 5.

questions.question: A model with R² = 0.80 explains ___ % of the answer.
questions.explanation: R² is a percentage. 0.80 = 80%.

questions.question:
Complete the Python code:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
score = ___(y_true, y_pred)
questions.explanation: Call the imported function: accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred).

questions.question: A bank wants to catch fraud. Missing a real fraud is very dangerous. The bank should care most about the metric called ___.
questions.explanation: When missing a YES case is costly, recall is the metric to maximise.
